title: Expected Value of a Function
short: E[g(X)] = Σ g(x) P(X = x), and in general E[g(X)] ≠ g(E[X]).
trouble: Students find E[X²] by squaring E[X].

blocks.html: The expected value $E[X] = \sum x\,P(X = x)$ is the long-run average of $X$. Often we need the average of something computed from $X$: a payoff, a square, a cost. There is no need to find the distribution of that new quantity first.

For a function $g$, $$\role[expected value]{integral}{E[g(X)]} = \sum_x \role[value of g]{output}{g(x)}\,\role[weight]{probability}{P(X = x)}.$$ Apply $g$ to each value, then weight by the probabilities. In general $E[g(X)] \ne g(E[X])$; they agree when $g(x) = ax + b$.

Let $Y = g(X)$. By definition $E[Y] = \sum_y y\,P(Y = y)$, and $P(Y = y)$ adds $P(X = x)$ over all $x$ with $g(x) = y$. So $$E[Y] = \sum_y \sum_{x:\,g(x) = y} g(x)\,P(X = x) = \sum_x g(x)\,P(X = x),$$ since every $x$ appears exactly once in the double sum. For a straight line, $$E[aX + b] = a\sum x\,p(x) + b\sum p(x) = aE[X] + b$$ For a curve there is no such shortcut.

head: $x$
blocks.cap: One fair die, with two functions of the roll.

blocks.title: The square of a die roll
blocks.q: Roll a fair die. Find $E[X^{2}]$ and compare it with $(E[X])^{2}$.
steps: They differ by $\frac{91}{6} - \frac{49}{4} = \frac{35}{12}$, which will turn out to be the variance.

blocks.title: A payoff
blocks.q: A game pays $\max(X - 4, 0)$ dollars on a fair die roll $X$: \$1 for a 5, \$2 for a 6, nothing otherwise. Find the expected payoff.
steps: Plugging in the mean gives $\max(3.5 - 4, 0) = 0$, which would call the game worthless.

blocks.html: The same rule handles any function the problems might use: $\lvert X - c \rvert$ (an average distance), $X(X - 1)$ (useful for counting pairs), $2^{X}$ (a doubling payoff) or $(X - c)^{2}$. In each case make a row of $g$-values, multiply by the probabilities, and add.

Finding $E[X^{2}]$ by squaring $E[X]$. Averaging and squaring do not commute: big values get squared into much bigger ones, so the average of the squares is larger. Check with a variable that is $-1$ or $1$ with equal chances: $E[X] = 0$, but $X^{2} = 1$ always, so $E[X^{2}] = 1$.
For a curve that bends upward (convex), such as $x^{2}$, $e^{x}$ or $\frac{1}{x}$ for $x > 0$, the inequality always goes one way: $E[g(X)] \ge g(E[X])$. This is Jensen's inequality.
